claim: KI cells lack all chemotactic activity.
source: we investigated collective cellular motion in a mutant strain of Dictyostelium discoideum, known as "KI cell," which lacks all chemotactic activity (Kuwayama and Ishida, 2013; Kuwayama et al., 1993)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kuwayama and Ishida, 2013 and Kuwayama et al., 1993

claim: KI cells do not form a cell aggregate under starvation conditions.
source: which lacks all chemotactic activity (Kuwayama and Ishida, 2013; Kuwayama et al., 1993), and thus does not form a cell aggregate under starvation conditions.
evidence: Stated as a consequence of lacking chemotactic activity, with citations

claim: Under starvation conditions, KI cells spread on a non-nutrient agar plate show a segregation of cell density which propagates as bands in around six hours.
source: Under starvation conditions, KI cells spread on a non-nutrient agar plate show a segregation of cell density, which propagates as bands in around six hours (Kuwayama and Ishida, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuwayama and Ishida, 2013

claim: Initially, the traveling bands propagate in random directions with high orientational persistence.
source: Initially, the traveling bands propagate in random directions with high orientational persistence.
evidence: Direct observation stated in the text

claim: When two bands collide, they appear to pass through each other, retaining their shapes.
source: When two bands collide, they appear to pass through each other, retaining their shapes (Figure 1a left) (Kuwayama and Ishida, 2013).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1a and citation to Kuwayama and Ishida, 2013

claim: Over time, the propagation directions of bands gradually become aligned, probably due to weak reorientation of propagation direction as an effect of collisions.
source: However, over time, the propagation directions gradually become aligned, probably due to weak reorientation of propagation direction as an effect of collisions.
evidence: Observation with speculative explanation

claim: Finally, the bands are arranged almost periodically in space with a spatial interval of about 1 mm.
source: Finally, the bands are arranged almost periodically in space with a spatial interval of about 1 mm (Figure 1a right, b).
evidence: Supported by Figure 1a and 1b showing periodic arrangement

claim: Cell migration speed inside the band is slightly faster than that outside the band.
source: The distribution of migration speeds indicates that cell migration speed inside the band is slightly faster than that outside the band (Figure 2b).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2b showing speed distributions

claim: The migration direction of cells inside the band was distributed around the direction of band propagation (176.2 degrees) with a standard deviation of 42.7 degrees.
source: The migration direction of the cells inside the band was distributed around the direction of band propagation (176.2 degrees, Figure 2c), although the fluctuation around the average direction is relatively large (standard deviation was 42.7 degrees).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from cell tracking analysis shown in Figure 2c

claim: The migration direction outside the band was distributed almost uniformly.
source: In contrast, the migration direction outside the band was distributed almost uniformly (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by Figure 2c showing uniform distribution

claim: Cells inside the band exhibit directionally persistent motions, whereas cells outside move randomly.
source: In sum, cells inside the band exhibit directionally persistent motions, whereas cells outside move randomly.
evidence: Summary statement based on MSD and directional analyses

claim: The band is continuously assembled at the front of the band and disassembled at the back.
source: This implies turnover of cells in the band, and that the band is continuously assembled at the front of the band and disassembled at the back.
evidence: Inference from the observation that band speed exceeds cell speed

claim: It is the cell density profile that shows propagation as a band.
source: Thus, it is the cell density profile that shows propagation as a band (Kuwayama and Ishida, 2013).
evidence: Conclusion from turnover analysis, supported by citation

claim: The high-density region is polar-ordered phase, which propagates in the low-density disordered phase.
source: Thus, the high-density region is polar-ordered phase, which propagates in the low-density disordered phase.
evidence: Conclusion based on polar order parameter measurements

claim: The polar order parameter of the band showed intersample variability, and was distributed from 0.6 to 0.85.
source: The polar order parameter of the band showed intersample variability, and was distributed from 0.6 to 0.85 (Figure 3b).
evidence: Measurement across multiple samples shown in Figure 3b

claim: The polar order phase is not completely homogeneous with respect to migration direction, but exhibits heterogeneity.
source: The polar order phase is not completely homogeneous with respect to migration direction, but exhibits heterogeneity; this is related to the underlying assembly mechanism.
evidence: Observation from optical flow analysis

claim: Within the band, the migration direction was widely distributed from about 145 to 210 degrees with a mean of 178.1 degrees and standard deviation of 31.2 degrees.
source: Within the band (Figure 3c bottom), the migration direction was widely distributed from about 145 to 210 degrees (a black line in Figure 3f; the mean is 178.1 degrees and the standard deviation is 31.2 degrees).
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3c and 3f

claim: There are two subpopulations within the band: one in which the migration direction is ~160 degrees and another in which it is ~190 degrees.
source: The probability density functions (pdf) of the migration direction obtained for the four regions (Figure 3c bottom (i–iv)) show peaks at different directions (Figure 3f), indicating the presence of two subpopulations; one in which the migration direction is ~160 degrees (regions (ii) and (iv)) and another in which it is ~190 degrees (regions (i) and (iii)).
evidence: Analysis of probability density functions shown in Figure 3f

claim: These two subpopulations form stripes that extend perpendicular to the direction of band propagation and are alternately arranged.
source: These two types of stripes extend perpendicular to the direction of band propagation, and are alternately arranged.
evidence: Observation from optical flow analysis

claim: The stripes are almost immobile.
source: The kymograph in Figure 3d shows the temporal evolution of the velocity field along the line PQ in Figure 3c, indicating that the stripes (light green and dark blue) are almost immobile
evidence: Kymograph analysis shown in Figure 3d

claim: The same cells experience the two stripes sequentially.
source: indicating that the stripes (light green and dark blue) are almost immobile, suggesting that the same cells experience the two stripes sequentially.
evidence: Inference from kymograph showing immobile stripes

claim: In low-density regions, cells are often associated with each other, migrating in single files.
source: In the low-density region, cells are not completely isolated, but rather are often associated with each other, migrating in single files (Figure 4a and Video 4).
evidence: Observation shown in Figure 4a and Video 4

claim: Tail-following behavior has been described for wild-type Dictyostelium cells within aggregation streams.
source: This tail-following behavior has been described for wild-type Dictyostelium cells within aggregation streams (Dormann et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dormann et al., 2002

claim: In half of the cases, cell–cell contact persists for more than 300 s.
source: As shown in Figure 4c, in half of the cases, cell–cell contact persists for more than 300 s.
evidence: Quantitative measurement shown in Figure 4c

claim: A knockout mutant that fails to express the cell–cell adhesion molecule TgrB1 exhibits reduced CFL activity.
source: A knockout mutant that fails to express the cell–cell adhesion molecule TgrB1 exhibits reduced CFL activity (Fujimori et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fujimori et al., 2019

claim: TgrB1 is known to mediate cell–cell adhesion via a heterophilic interaction with its partner TgrC1.
source: TgrB1 is known to mediate cell–cell adhesion via a heterophilic interaction with its partner TgrC1 (Hirose et al., 2011; Hirose et al., 2015; Li et al., 2015; Fujimori et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: In the tgrB1 null mutant, neither segregation of cell density nor propagating bands appeared.
source: However, neither segregation of cell density nor propagating bands appeared (Videos 6 and 7).
evidence: Observation shown in Videos 6 and 7

claim: In the tgrB1 null mutant, in 80% of all cases, cell–cell contact is disrupted before 300 s.
source: We found that in 80% of all cases, cell–cell contact is disrupted before 300 s (Figure 4f)
evidence: Quantitative measurement shown in Figure 4f

claim: In the tgrB1 null mutant, only 10% of cells established CFL.
source: and that only 10% of cells established CFL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Quantitative measurement shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d

claim: In the tgrb1 null mutant, CFL is nearly absent.
source: Thus, our analyses illustrate that in the tgrb1 null mutant, CFL is nearly absent.
evidence: Conclusion from quantitative measurements of contact duration and CFL angle

claim: CFL is essential for the segregation of cell density and the formation of propagating bands.
source: The above analyses suggest that the difference in the cellular scale behavior between control KI cell and tgrb1 mutant cell is the ability of CFL, and we thus conclude that CFL is essential for the segregation of cell density and the formation of propagating bands.
evidence: Conclusion based on comparison between KI cells and tgrB1 mutant

claim: In the simulation, the speeds of the traveling band and particles within the band were 0.96 and 0.9, respectively, relative to the speed of isolated particles.
source: The speeds of the traveling band and particles within the band were 0.96 and 0.9, respectively, relative to the speed of isolated particles, indicating that the band is dynamic with assembly in the front and disassembly in the tail, consistent with our experimental results.
evidence: Quantitative results from simulation with interpretation

claim: The formation of internal structure appears to be a characteristic of the collective behavior induced by CFL.
source: Thus, the formation of internal structure appears to be a characteristic of the collective behavior induced by CFL.
evidence: Conclusion from comparison between CFL-induced and alignment-induced bands in simulation

claim: Wildtype Dictyostelium discoideum forms an aggregate as a result of chemotaxis mediated by a self-secreted extracellular chemoattractant.
source: Wildtype Dictyostelium discoideum forms an aggregate as a result of chemotaxis mediated by a self-secreted extracellular chemoattractant.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about wildtype behavior

claim: The collective migration of eukaryotic cells plays crucial roles in processes such as wound healing, tumor progression, and morphogenesis.
source: The collective migration of eukaryotic cells plays crucial roles in processes such as wound healing, tumor progression, and morphogenesis, and has been the focus of extensive study (Haeger et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Haeger et al., 2015

claim: Contact inhibition of locomotion is a mechanism by which cells migrate away from the contact site.
source: One mechanism that induces cells to correlate their motions is contact inhibition of locomotion, by which cells migrating away from the contact site.
evidence: Statement of established mechanism

claim: Tail-following behavior at the contact site is termed contact following locomotion (CFL).
source: Here, we report that tail-following behavior at the contact site, termed contact following locomotion (CFL), can induce a non-trivial collective behavior in migrating cells.
evidence: Definition provided in the abstract

claim: CFL enables a theoretical description of how the traveling band forms.
source: We find that CFL is the cell–cell interaction underlying this phenomenon, enabling a theoretical description of how this traveling band forms.
evidence: Conclusion stated in abstract based on experimental and modeling results

claim: The polar order phase consists of subpopulations that exhibit characteristic transversal motions with respect to the direction of band propagation.
source: We further show that the polar order phase consists of subpopulations that exhibit characteristic transversal motions with respect to the direction of band propagation.
evidence: Finding stated in abstract based on optical flow analysis

claim: The local cell density within the band is similar across different samples.
source: The local cell density within the band is similar across different samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c)
evidence: Observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c

claim: If the correlation in the migration direction is gradually decorrelated from the front to the end of the band, bands with lower order parameters will be more prone to larger decorrelation in the migration direction.
source: We speculate that if the correlation in the migration direction is gradually decorrelated from the front to the end of the band, bands with lower order parameters will be more prone to larger decorrelation in the migration direction.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed correlation

claim: During the relative movement of cells from the front to the end of band, the migration direction may not be dampened completely to the direction of band propagation probably due to the directional persistence induced by CFL.
source: During the relative movement of these cells from the front to the end of band, the migration direction may not be dampened completely to the direction of band propagation probably due to the directional persistence induced by CFL.
evidence: Speculative explanation for internal structure formation

claim: Subpopulations with respect to the migration direction are formed when CFL is present.
source: In this way, subpopulations with respect to the migration direction are formed when CFL is present.
evidence: Conclusion based on speculation about directional persistence

claim: It has been suggested that other mechanisms also involve in the formation of aggregate, such as contact following.
source: It has been suggested, however, that other mechanism also involves in the formation of aggregate, such as contact following (Dormann et al., 2002; Fujimori et al., 2019; Shaffer, 1962; Umeda and Inouye, 2002).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: KI cells are able to spontaneously migrate to the central tip region transplanted from a wildtype slug and undergo normal morphogenesis and cell differentiation.
source: In fact, whereas the KI cell alone does not form the multicellular structure, KI cells are able to spontaneously migrate to the central tip region transplanted from a wildtype slug and undergo normal morphogenesis and cell differentiation; this is not observed in mutant KI cells lacking TgrB1 (Kida et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kida et al., 2019

claim: TgrB1-dependent CFL without chemotaxis allows KI cells to spontaneously migrate in slug.
source: this is not observed in mutant KI cells lacking TgrB1 (Kida et al., 2019), suggesting that TgrB1-dependent CFL without chemotaxis allows KI cells to spontaneously migrate in slug.
evidence: Inference from comparison between KI cells and TgrB1-lacking KI cells, supported by citation

claim: In wildtype cells, the chemical guidance cue has been shown to cease during the multicellular phase.
source: Furthermore, in wildtype cells, the chemical guidance cue has been shown to cease during the multicellular phase, which suggests that an alternative mechanism induces collective cell migration in the multicellular body (Hashimura et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hashimura et al., 2019

claim: Polar order formation induced by CFL plays an important role in late-stage morphogenesis in Dictyostelium discoideum.
source: We propose that polar order formation induced by CFL plays an important role in late-stage morphogenesis in this organism.
evidence: Proposal based on findings about CFL and observations in wildtype cells

claim: Contact following locomotion, or chain migration, have been reported in other cell types.
source: Contact following locomotion, or chain migration, have been reported in other cell types (Li and Wang, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li and Wang, 2018

claim: The macroscopic behaviors reported in this paper may be found in other systems as well.
source: The macroscopic behaviors reported in this paper may thus be found in other systems as well.
evidence: Speculation based on the fact that CFL is reported in other cell types

claim: The time scale that cells pass across a stripe is about 200-400 s.
source: Thus, the time scale that cells pass across a stripe is about 200-400 s, if the stripe is almost immobile as we have shown above.
evidence: Calculation based on cell speed and stripe width

claim: The time interval that cells travel across the traveling band is obtained as 1120 s.
source: The time interval that cells travel across the traveling band is obtained as 1120 s.
evidence: Calculation from experimental data

claim: Cells pass several different stripes during the time interval that cells stay in the traveling band.
source: Thus, cells pass several different stripes during the time interval that cells stay in the traveling band.
evidence: Inference from time scale calculations
